newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Congo's Lissouba ignores war to spend day abroad.
newsitem.headline: Congo's Lissouba ignores war to spend day abroad.

text.p: Congo's President Pascal Lissouba left his capital Brazzaville on Monday for the first time since a civil war broke out three weeks ago, flying over for national day festivities in Laurent Kabila's "other" Congo.

A spokesman said Lissouba took a short flight to the twin capital of Kinshasa across the Congo river, a sign his government forces are in full control of Brazzaville airport over which a heavy battle was fought last week.
The president of the former French Congo joined Kabila and six other African heads of state to celebrate independence day in what used to be the Belgian Congo.
A spokesman said he returned safely through the airport before nightfall.
Brazzaville remained relatively calm on Monday, the third day of a new ceasefire between Lissouba and Sassou.
Witnesses said there had been some shooting in the city centre that is now a no man's land, as well as a bout of mysterious shelling in the middle of the night.
"It woke me up at about three o'clock. We've got no idea who was firing," one expatriate told Reuters.
French ambassador Raymond Cesaire, the only foreign envoy left in the capital of Lissouba's oil-rich central African country, reported some isolated shooting around his embassy.
The former colonial city, wartime capital for "Free French" leader General Charles de Gaulle, has been devastated by shelling, street battles and looting since June 5.
Aid workers estimate some 1,000 to 3,000 people, mostly civilians, have died in a conflict that has wavered between merciless artillery duels and truces that bring only relative and partial calm.
A lasting political solution seems no nearer.
Both Lissouba and Sassou say they want free and fair presidential elections, but disagree on how to hold them.
Sassou's Radio Congo Freedom said that planeloads of Serb, Liberian and Angolan opposition UNITA mercenaries were flooding into the country to help Lissouba.

International mediation efforts led by Omar Bongo, president of neighbouring Gabon, have centred on the dispatch of an African intervention force but the United Nations says there must be a lasting peace first.
